It is written here, with regard to Shabbat: “And I will cause you to ride on the heights [bamotei] of the world” (Isaiah 58:14), and it is written there: “You are fortunate Israel, who is like you? A nation redeemed by God, the shield that aids you and the sword of your triumph. Your enemies will try to defeat you and you will trample their high places [bamoteimo]” (Deuteronomy 33:29). Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: With regard to anyone who delights in the Shabbat, God grants him his heart’s desires, as it is stated: “And you shall delight in God…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 118b) to illuminate his argument here (“And regarding this the Talmud states (Shabbat 118b): Had Israel kept two Sabbaths properly, they would have been redeemed immediately; the meaning being: the first Sabbath is the direct acknowledgment of the second...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And "If Israel kept two Shabbats they would be redeemed" (Shabbat 118b): one may say this refers to man's primary labor being in concrete action with the limbs through which all commandments and prohibitions of the Torah are fulfilled, and all sins being ascribed to the Nefesh: "if a soul sins" [Leviticus 5:1], for sin occurs in action where in the world of Asiyah evil dominates as is known; and likewise in the emotional traits of the heart where the Ruach dwells in Yetzirah, where good and evil are balanced as is known, for there is the abode of the two inclinations: "a wise man's heart is at his right, but a fool's heart at his left" [Ecclesiastes 10:2]…
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 30:31–32
column15: Therefore concerning him it is written (Isaiah 58:14): “And I will feed you the heritage of Jacob your father,” which the Sages expounded (Shabbat 118b): an inheritance without boundaries—incessant and limitless, with divine bounty renewing within him at every moment.

column11: Deuteronomy 32:15: ‘So Jeshurun grew fat and kicked—You grew fat and gross and coarse uncertain.—They forsook the God who made themAnd spurned the Rock of their support.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 32:15) to illuminate his argument here (“whereby "you waxed fat, you grew thick, you became gorged" Deuteronomy 32:15, and as in Berakhot (32a): "You caused this through abundance; what can the son do and not sin?"; for because Hashem declares that all is...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Except that if they sink themselves into this [worldly abundance] alone, they will come, Heaven forbid, to be sundered from His unity, in the sense of “you grew fat — and he forsook [the God who made him]” (Devarim 32:15), , ” — “and Yeshurun grew fat and kicked — you grew fat, thick, gross — and he forsook the God who made him, and spurned the Rock of his salvation.” Background: from the song of Ha’azinu — Moshe’s warning that material abundance would lead Israel to rebel. Meforshim: the verse itself traces the descent — satiety (“you grew fat”) breeds “kicking” against Heaven, which ends in forsaking God; wealth ungoverned by gratitude produces rebellion.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 57:16–19
column15: And as in Zohar (Pekudei 260a): The Full Name is “Havayah Elohim,” and man is the one who binds them together. For in truth, after all the arduous labors that man performs for Hashem, Scripture states (Deuteronomy 32:36): “When He sees that their power is gone” — meaning man will perceive clearly that he achieved nothing on his own, and then the Blessed Name will reveal that man was never able to transgress His ultimate Will, all stemming from Him.

column11: Berakhot 32a: ‘On a similar note, Rav Aḥa, son of Rav Huna, said that Rav Sheshet said: That is what people say in a popular maxim: Filling his stomach is a type of sin, as it is stated: “When they were fed and became full they were sated, and their hearts were lifted and they have forgotten Me” (Hosea 13:6). Rav Naḥman said: This principle is derived not from the verse in Hosea, but from here: “And your heart is lifted and you forget the Lord” (Deuteronomy 8:14). And the Rabbis say that this principle is derived from here: “And they will have eaten and been sated and fattened, and they will turn to other gods” (Deuteronomy 31:20).’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 32a) to illuminate his argument here (“and as in Berakhot (32a): "You caused this through abundance; what can the son do and not sin?"; for because Hashem declares that all is Israel's ("the earth has He given to mankind"), through this abundance one may...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: [who was called Our Holy Master because he derived no personal worldly enjoyment, even though it was said in Avodah Zarah (11a) that radish and lettuce never departed from his table, because all of it was elevated in sanctity]; for sated fullness arising from physical appetite lacking holiness drags sin in its wake, as stated in Berakhot (32a): "A full stomach breeds corrupt sorts," and as written: "Lest when you have eaten and are full... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget..." column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 3
column15: And Hashem said in His heart: I will not again curse the ground anymore for man's sake, etc. Behold, this thought of Hashem, blessed be He, became known to Noah inasmuch as profound awe was ingrained in his heart after the Deluge, that it is inappropriate for man to expand himself unchecked according to his own desire, and he must only restrain his spirit; from this he understood that such was likewise the will of Hashem, blessed be He, that He would not curse the ground anymore.

column11: Bava Batra 75b: ‘With regard to the righteous, this is as we have just said. With regard to the Messiah, this is as it is written: “And this is his name whereby he shall be called, the Lord is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6). With regard to Jerusalem, this is as it is written: “It shall be eighteen thousand reeds round about. And the name of the city from that day shall be, the Lord is there [shamma]” (Ezekiel 48:35). Do not read the word as “there” [shamma]; rather, read it as: The Lord is its name [shemah]. Rabbi Elazar says: In the future, the righteous will have the name: Holy, recited before them, as one recites before the Holy One, Blessed be He; as it is stated: “And it shall come to pass, that…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 75b) to illuminate his argument here (“as written (Bava Batra 75b): The righteous are destined to be called by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He. And this is the dispute in Shabbat (69b) regarding one lost in the wilderness who forgets the Sabbath:...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Whence derives the root of the yetzer tov: to cleave unto the Blessed Name and walk in His pathways: "as He is merciful, so be you merciful, etc." (Shabbat 133b), to resemble Him; and as the Sages stated (Bava Batra 75b): "In the Future the righteous will be called by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He"; and just as He revives the dead and remembers the barren, so do the righteous (Bereishis Rabbah 77:1).
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 5
column15: And it shall come to pass, when I bring a cloud over the earth, that the bow shall be seen in the cloud. 'Cloud' signifies awe and concealment, and 'bow' signifies mighty trust; for amid all the intensity of fear, you shall possess great trust, and this the Holy One, blessed be He, promised to Noah. And this is what is stated in the holy Zohar (Bereishit 72b): 'Do not look for the footsteps of the Messiah until you see the bow glowing with radiant colors,' meaning when the divine fortitude from Hashem, blessed be He, stands prominent and explicit before your eyes, then anticipate the footsteps of the Messiah.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6
column11: Shabbat 69b: ‘Rav Huna said: One who was walking along the way or in the desert, and he does not know when Shabbat occurs, he counts six days from the day that he realized that he lost track of Shabbat and then observes one day as Shabbat. Ḥiyya bar Rav says: He first observes one day as Shabbat and then he counts six weekdays. The Gemara explains: With regard to what do they disagree? One Sage, Rav Huna, held: It is like the creation of the world, weekdays followed by Shabbat. And one Sage, Ḥiyya bar Rav, held: It is like Adam, the first man, who was created on the sixth day. He observed Shabbat followed by the six days of the week. The Gemara raises an objection to the opinion of Ḥiyya bar Rav from…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 69b) to illuminate his argument here (“And this is the dispute in Shabbat (69b) regarding one lost in the wilderness who forgets the Sabbath: does he count six days and observe the seventh, or vice versa: one master deriving from the Creation of the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And through this will be understood the Tannaitic disputes in Shabbat (69b): whether one lost in the wilderness counts six days and sanctifies the seventh, or conversely sanctifies the first day and counts six; depending on whether we derive the sequence from the Creation of the world (where six workdays preceded the first Sabbath) or from Adam the first man (who was created on the sixth day and immediately entered the Sabbath).
column14: Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 4:3
column15: “One beyond number” refers to that which is entirely above the grasp of creation; and “One within number” refers to His manifestation within the framework of creation. And this is what the Midrash asks: “If it is according to the count of days,” meaning since creation has already begun here, it ought to have said “a first day” [in series]; and the Midrash answers: Rather, from the time when the Holy One, blessed be He, was completely alone in His world, He yearned to possess a dwelling place among the lower realms.

column11: Pesachim 7b: ‘The Gemara poses a question: In any event, it is clear from the previous discussion that everyone agrees that one is required to recite a blessing prior to performing a mitzva. From where do we derive this principle? It is as Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said: With regard to all the mitzvot, one recites a blessing over them prior to [over] their performance.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 7b) to illuminate his argument here (“just as all blessings over mitzvot are instituted prior to execution (Pesachim 7b), failure to bless constituting sacrilege; and after enjoyment, being satisfied, he recites the Grace After Meals, which corresponds...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column12: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 1:23 (§4)
column13: In the same way, the blessings established over all bodily pleasures were instituted to be recited immediately prior to the act of enjoyment, affirming that "the earth and all its fullness belong to Hashem." And only following the recitation of the blessing does the verse apply: "The earth He has given to the children of men," as taught in Berakhot (35a–b), whereafter one is permitted to derive benefit, having recognized from the outset that everything originates from Hashem.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Beshalach 12:6
column15: However, women are required to perform mitzvot that are not bound to time, and this is the sign that this Kedusha is fixed in the hearts of Israel.Knowing this, Moshe had them move on, for whenever it is not yet fixed in the heart of man he can still enter into uncertainty, and enter this Kedusha into uncertainty, for it is not yet promised to him, so he may enter it into uncertainty on the possibility that he may gain even more.

column11: Berakhot 35a: ‘MISHNA: This mishna discusses the blessings recited over various foods. How does one recite a blessing over fruits? Over different fruits that grow on a tree one recites: Who creates fruit of the tree, with the exception of wine. Although wine is produced from fruit of the tree, due to its significance, its blessing differs from other fruits of the tree. Over wine one recites: Who creates fruit of the vine. Over fruits that grow from the earth, one recites: Who creates fruit of the ground, with the exception of bread. Bread, too, is significant and its blessing differs from other fruits of the ground, as over bread one recites: Who brings forth bread from the earth. Over herbs and leafy…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 35a) to illuminate his argument here (“just as all blessings over mitzvot are instituted prior to execution (Pesachim 7b), failure to bless constituting sacrilege; and after enjoyment, being satisfied, he recites the Grace After Meals, which corresponds...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And this is the ordinance of our Sages in blessings over all bodily pleasures: food, sight, hearing like the rooster's crow, good tidings and their opposite, garments, and the like. And this is the opening of the Talmud (Tractate Berakhot), which is the root of the entire Torah, mirroring the opening of the Written Torah with "I am" and "You shall have no," which encapsulate the whole Torah, the rest being commentary—go and learn: various counsels for every time and place how to attain this remembrance.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 34:1–4
column15: “And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree.” Behold, just as a distinction exists between grass and herbs—which endure merely for a single season and not permanently— and trees, which possess lasting permanence from being firmly planted initially, whereupon the sap continually ascends to nourish them, and they reproduce perpetually from their seed sown in the soil without ever ceasing—.

column11: Berakhot 57b: ‘The numbers five, six, and ten are mnemonics for the categories to follow. The Gemara says: There are five matters in our world which are one-sixtieth of their most extreme manifestations. They are: Fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and a dream. The Gemara elaborates: Our fire is one-sixtieth of the fire of Gehenna; honey is one-sixtieth of manna; Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World-to-Come; sleep is one-sixtieth of death; and a dream is one-sixtieth of prophecy.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 57b) to illuminate his argument here (“The Sabbath is one-sixtieth of the World to Come, as written in Berakhot (57b); the World to Come being the cessation of work—"this day to do them, and not tomorrow to do them" Eruvin 22a— where "the righteous sit...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: A good man meriting the blessing: "you shall behold your world in your lifetime" (Berachos 17a); experiencing a foretaste of the World to Come, which is the essence of divine sanctification from Above; like the holiness of Shabbat which is a foretaste of the World to Come, one-sixtieth thereof. And tzaddikim in old age perceive this with ever greater intensity; though during life it is not held as an absolute acquisition but as visual perception ("you shall behold your world").
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 12:26–28
column15: And to this points Berakhot (14a): “Whoever sleeps seven days without a dream is called evil”; a dream mirroring the Sabbath light uniting lower and higher realms (Zohar Vayeitzei 149b; Berakhot 57b); hinting that throughout the cycle of seven, one who fails to connect his six active attributes to the divine Will is called evil, clinging to an isolated trait.

column11: Eruvin 22a: ‘And that is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “And you shall keep the commandments, and the statutes, and the judgments which I command you today to do them” (Deuteronomy 7:11)? It means: Today is the time to do them, in this world, and tomorrow is not the time to do them, as there is no obligation or opportunity to fulfill mitzvot in the World-to-Come. Furthermore, it means: Today is the time to do them, but only tomorrow, in the ultimate future, is the time to receive reward for doing them.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 22a) to illuminate his argument here (“the World to Come being the cessation of work—"this day to do them, and not tomorrow to do them" Eruvin 22a— where "the righteous sit with crowns on their heads, delighting in the radiance of the Shechinah" (Berakhot...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: But every matter is divided into six levels as is known, each one incorporating a specific rung: matching the seven days of Creation: six days of action, and the seventh day Shabbos which is a foretaste of the World to Come, and likewise the six thousand years of this world; so too is it in the World to Come, which is the time of receiving the reward for deeds: for the days of action of this world, of "today to perform them" (Eruvin 22a), constitute six rungs.

column15: Allowing them to expand in willful lust upon that false security. "And from there Hashem scattered them" (Genesis 11:8)— meaning: what value is this peace that you forged among yourselves?! And although it is a great matter that My Name is called Peace, as in the Talmud (Shabbat 10b), yet your entire design is that through this you erase My Name!

column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘After his prayer, Rabbi Alexandri said the following: May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You station us in a lighted corner and not in a darkened corner, and do not let our hearts become faint nor our eyes dim. Some say that this was the prayer that Rav Hamnuna would recite, and that after Rabbi Alexandri prayed, he would say the following: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to perform Your will, and what prevents us? On the one hand, the yeast in the dough, the evil inclination that is within every person; and the subjugation to the kingdoms on the other. May it be Your will that You will deliver us from their hands, of both the evil…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his argument here (“where "the righteous sit with crowns on their heads, delighting in the radiance of the Shechinah" (Berakhot 17a); and so in microcosm on the Sabbath, even though "there is no reward for mitzvot in this world"...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: For in the World to Come there is no eating or drinking, but the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah (Berachos 17a); and "I shall be satisfied, when I awake" denotes attaining this very satiation within this world; and through this, death thereafter is merely like falling asleep, which is likewise a state of not dying, except that his immortality remains concealed.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 9
column15: "And he said: O Lord God, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?" (Genesis 15:8). For Avraham requested of Hashem, blessed be He: after all the spiritual clarifications wherein the Shechinah was revealed through him in the world, yet 'whereby shall I know?' meaning: how shall this consciousness become permanently engraved within my heart without any interruption? And to this He answered him: "Take for Me a heifer of three years old, and a she-goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old..."

column11: Kiddushin 39b: ‘The Gemara asks: But perhaps he was contemplating idol worship at the time, and it is written with regard to idol worship: “So I may take the house of Israel in their own heart” (Ezekiel 14:5), which indicates that one is punished for idolatrous thoughts. The Gemara answers: Rabbi Ya’akov was saying this as well: If it enters your mind that there is reward for performing a mitzva in this world, why didn’t these mitzvot protect him so that he should not come to contemplate idol worship? Since that man was not protected from thoughts of idol worship at the time, this indicates that the performance of mitzvot does not entitle one to merit reward in this world.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 39b) to illuminate his argument here (“and so in microcosm on the Sabbath, even though "there is no reward for mitzvot in this world" (Kiddushin 39b). Therefore it is said: "The Sabbath is a precious gift in My treasury," as written in Shabbat (10b), and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Shabbos also has the aspect of 'lending': its holiness implants sanctity in the coming weekdays so that they too become holy. This enables a person to keep the following Shabbos properly. The weekdays in turn lead to an ever-deepening sanctity of Shabbos from week to week. This is the aspect of lending. Thus Rabbi Chiyya says, 'All are one; all stated a single teaching.' Every interpreter explains 'gracious and lending' in terms of the outpouring of the good light that Hashem grants to 'Kol,' as in 'Hashem is good to all.'

column15: “And God spoke to Moshe saying, take for Me an offering [truma] ….” (Shemot, 25:2)This is as it is written (Yesahya, 45:1), “Thus spoke God … who formed the land … He did not create a desolation for his creations to dwell in…” In Parshat Yitro, when Israel heard the Ten Mitzvot, it was easy for them to fulfill them since these mitzvot depend on the actions of man.

column11: Shabbat 10b: ‘Incidental to the halakhic statement in his name, the Gemara also cites another statement that Rava bar Meḥasseya said that Rav Ḥama bar Gurya said that Rav said: One who gives a gift to another must inform him that he is giving it to him. column13: This is the meaning of the teaching (Shabbat 10b): 'I have a good gift in My treasure-house, and Shabbat is its name,' and so forth. That is, as they said (Berakhot 33b): the Holy One, blessed be He, has no treasure, as it were, except a treasury of fear of Heaven; this is His treasure-house. For a king's treasures are his possessions, on account of which his kingship is expressed.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 9:2
column15: The concept is: behold, Peace is the Name of the Holy One, as brought in the Talmud (Shabbat 10b), and that is because Hashem is complete in all perfection, and all wholeness found in the world derives from Hashem, and within the attribute of Peace are included all blessings.

column11: Berakhot 33b: ‘The verse says: What does the Lord your God ask of you other than to fear the Lord your God. The Gemara asks: Is fear of Heaven a minor matter that it can be presented as if God is not asking anything significant? Didn’t Rabbi Ḥanina say in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: The Holy One, Blessed be He, has nothing in his treasury other than a treasure of fear of Heaven, as it is stated: “Fear of the Lord is his treasure” (Isaiah 33:6). The Lord values and treasures fear of Heaven over all else.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 33b) to illuminate his argument here (“and He said "in My treasury," and the Holy One possesses in His storehouse nothing other than the treasure of the fear of Heaven (Berakhot 33b), and within that treasure of awe the Sabbath is hidden. For awe is the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Yet in ultimate truth, "You have wrought all our works for us," and "All is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven" (Berakhot 33b) which resides solely in the heart, as expounded in Yoma [72b] on "and has no heart," meaning one who acknowledges that he possesses nothing of himself and that all derives from Hashem, except that the Blessed Name willed that we toil so that accomplishments be credited to our name and we not eat unearned bread of shame (Jerusalem Talmud, Orlah 1).
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 6
column15: And the whole earth was of one language and of few words. And Scripture does not state 'one tongue' (lashon), for the primary essence of 'tongue' is the Holy Tongue, because the Holy Tongue stems from that which is ingrained in the depth of the heart and wells forth from the root of vitality; while all other tongues are termed the language of stammerers, as it is written (Isaiah 33:19): "a stammering tongue that one cannot understand", meaning it possesses no life-root in the heart, for understanding resides in the heart; and the Generation of the Division, though they spoke the Holy Tongue, nonetheless lacked the inner vitality, speaking it merely from…

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7
column11: Yoma 72b: ‘The Gemara asks: But wasn’t it taught in a baraita that the outer ark was eleven handbreadths and a bit? The Gemara explains: This is not difficult: This statement in the baraita is in accordance with the one who said that the thickness of the gold plating was one handbreadth. According to this opinion, the outer ark’s base took up one handbreadth of its height, ten handbreadths were then needed to contain the middle ark within it, and then a bit more was needed so it could also contain the Ark’s cover. That statement of Rav Yehuda is in accordance with the one who said that the thickness of the gold plating was not one handbreadth but was a plate of gold of negligible thickness.…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his argument here (“For awe is the purity of the heart, as known from Yoma (72b) on the verse "seeing he has no heart" Proverbs 17:16, wherefore the Congregation of Israel is titled "Awe" (Yirah) in Kabbalah; for the nations have a...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
